paper_context.research_question: Can financial disclosure sentiments, processed with word embedding-based Information Retrieval models and fused with market data, effectively predict stock market volatility, and what are the characteristics of these predictions across different financial sectors?
main_claims: A word embedding-based Information Retrieval term weighting approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for volatility prediction using financial disclosure sentiments.

Effective fusion methods combining textual sentiment features from 10-K reports with factual market data (e.g., GARCH, current volatility) further improve volatility prediction accuracy and stability over longer terms.
The content of 10-K reports exhibits conceptual drifts over time, making more recent data (e.g., 2012-2015) more effective for current volatility prediction.

While financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics, training sector-specific models does not improve performance over a general model due to limited training data size per sector, though sector-agnostic models reveal the importance of sector-specific factors.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Novelty and effectiveness of the proposed word embedding-based IR term weighting models for sentiment analysis in financial disclosures.
Robustness and performance of the proposed feature fusion methods (early, late, MKL) in combining textual and market data for volatility prediction.
Rigour of experimental setup, including dataset construction, baseline comparisons, and evaluation metrics (r2, MSE).
Depth and insightfulness of the analysis of 10-K report content changes over time and across different financial sectors.
Generalizability of the findings to different time periods or financial markets.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The content of 10-K reports exhibits conceptual drifts over time, making more recent data (e.g., 2012-2015) more effective for current volatility prediction by reducing noise.
extracted_claims.section_anchor: 1 Introduction, 6.1 Content Analysis of 10-K Reports, Figure 1a, Figure 1b

extracted_claims.claim_label: Sector-Specific Models Underperform Due to Data Size
extracted_claims.claim_text: While financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics, training sector-specific models does not improve performance over a general model due to limited training data size per sector.
evidence: "despite the reasonable expectation that domain-specific training would lead to improvements, we show that our general model generalizes well and outperforms sector-specific trained models."
Figures 3a and 3b show 'Sector-specific' bars are consistently lower than 'General model' bars for both Text and Text+Market features.

"Results also confirm the hypothesis that the data for training in each sector is simply too small, and as additional data is accumulated, we can further improve on the results by training on different sectors independently."

extracted_claims.claim_text: Comparison between sector-agnostic and sector-specific models (trained on same-sized subsets) reveals the existence and importance of particular risk factors in each sector.
evidence: "The large performance differences between sector-agnostic and -specific show the existence of particular risk factors in each sector and their importance."

Figures 3a and 3b show 'Sector-agnostic' models (trained on random samples of the same size as sector-specific data) generally perform better than 'Sector-specific' models, implying that the general data contains more relevant signals even for specific sectors, but also that sector-specific factors exist.

extracted_claims.claim_text: The proposed extended IR term weighting schemes (e.g., B̂M25, T̂C, T̂FIDF, T̂F), which incorporate word embeddings, generally improve upon their normal forms (BM25, TC, TFIDF, TF) for volatility prediction.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Among the tested feature fusion methods, stacking outperforms MKL and Early Fusion in terms of both r2 and MSE for combining textual and market features.

extracted_claims.claim_text: Sector-specific models can mitigate word ambiguity and context-dependent sentiment issues present in general lexicons, as the variety of word senses is more restricted within a sector.
evidence: "For instance, the keyword fire has a high coefficient in the energy sector, but very low in the others. identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 'Risk Factors' section (Item 1A) of 10-K reports is the most useful and informative part for investors regarding company risk and volatility prediction, justifying its exclusive use for textual analysis.
supporting_evidence: "Dyer et al. (2016) ... suggest that only the risk factors topic appears to be useful and informative to investors. Their analysis motivates us to study the effectiveness of the Risk Factors section for volatility prediction."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If other sections of 10-K reports contain significant, non-redundant, and useful information for volatility prediction, the model's performance might be suboptimal due to incomplete textual feature extraction.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The definition of volatility as the natural log of the standard deviation of (adjusted) return prices over a τ-day window (realized volatility) is an appropriate and sufficient measure for financial market instability and risk in this context.
supporting_evidence: "Similar to previous studies (Christiansen et al., 2012; Kogan et al., 2009; Tsai and Wang, 2014), volatility is defined as the natural log of the standard deviation of (adjusted) return prices in a window of τ days. This definition is referred to as standard volatility (Li and Hong, 2011) or realized volatility (Liu and TSE, 2013)."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If this specific definition of volatility does not fully capture the relevant aspects of financial instability or risk, the predictions, while accurate for the defined target, may not fully align with broader financial risk assessment needs.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The finance-specific lexicon by Loughran and McDonald (2011), potentially expanded by Word2Vec, adequately captures the sentiment relevant for financial volatility prediction.
supporting_evidence: "Similar to previous studies (Nopp and Hanbury, 2015; Wang et al., 2013), we extract the keyword set from a finance-specific lexicon (Loughran and McDonald, 2011) using the positive, negative, and uncertain groups, stemmed using the Porter stemmer."
"Tsai and Wang (2014) expanded this set by adding the top 20 related terms to each term to the original set. ... We also use this expanded set in our experiments and refer to it as LexExt."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the lexicon misses crucial sentiment terms or misclassifies terms in the specific context of 10-K reports, the sentiment features derived may be incomplete or inaccurate, affecting prediction performance.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The chosen parameters for Support Vector Regression (C=1.0, ε=0.1) and the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel are optimal or sufficiently robust for the volatility prediction task across all experiments.
supporting_evidence: "Similar to previous studies (Tsai and Wang, 2014; Kogan et al., 2009), we set C = 1.0 and = 0.1."
"Our initial experiments showed better performance of the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel in comparison to linear and cosine kernels and is therefore used in this paper."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Suboptimal parameter choices or kernel selection could lead to lower-than-achievable prediction performance or reduced generalizability of the models.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The NASDAQ categorization of financial sectors is an appropriate and sufficiently granular classification for analyzing sector-specific risk factors and training sector-specific models.
supporting_evidence: "Sector is the sector that the corresponding company of the report belongs to, namely energy (ene), basic industries (ind), finance (fin), technology (tech), miscellaneous (misc), consumer nondurables (n-dur), consumer durables (dur), capital goods (capt), consumer services (serv), public utilities (pub), and health care (hlth)1. The feature is converted to numerical representation using onehot encoding. 1We follow NASDAQ categorization of sectors."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the NASDAQ categorization is too broad or misaligns with actual risk factor commonalities, the sector-specific analysis and conclusions about data size limitations might be skewed.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Filtering volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation effectively removes noise/outliers without discarding meaningful extreme volatility events that could be important for risk prediction.
supporting_evidence: "We filter the volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation of all the volatility values3."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If these filtered values represent genuine, albeit extreme, market behavior, their removal could lead to a model that is less robust in predicting high-impact, rare events.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 2012-2015 dataset, identified as the 'most coherent and largest data' and 'most recent cluster' after content analysis, is sufficiently representative for generalizing findings to future reports and market conditions.
supporting_evidence: "As shown, the most coherent and largest data consists of the subset of the reports published between 2012 to 2015. This subset is also the most recent cluster and presumably more similar to the future reports. Therefore, in the following, we only use this subset, which consists of 3892 reports, belonging to 1323 companies."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If future conceptual drifts occur or if the 2012-2015 period is not representative of broader market dynamics, the generalizability of the model's performance and insights may be limited.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The use of Principle Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce feature vector dimensions to 400 is optimal and does not lead to significant loss of predictive information.
supporting_evidence: "Our initial experiments show 400 dimension as the optimum by trying on a range of dimensions from 50 to 1000."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the optimal dimension was not thoroughly explored or if PCA discards crucial non-linear information, the model's performance could be suboptimal.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The Porter stemmer is appropriate for financial text, and its stemming rules do not introduce significant semantic loss or ambiguity for sentiment analysis, particularly for risk-sensitive terms.
supporting_evidence: "Finally, the texts are stemmed using the Porter stemmer."
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Over-stemming or under-stemming could lead to incorrect term matching, loss of nuanced meaning, or increased ambiguity, thereby negatively impacting sentiment feature quality and prediction accuracy.

chaining_notes: Reviewers should critically assess the theoretical grounding and empirical novelty of the word embedding-based IR term weighting approach, particularly its distinction from prior art using word embeddings for lexicon expansion.

The effectiveness and practical implications of the chosen fusion methods, especially stacking, should be scrutinized, considering its potential limitations (e.g., data split for training base and meta models).
The analysis of conceptual drift and the subsequent decision to use only 2012-2015 data warrants attention, particularly regarding the generalizability of findings to earlier or future periods.
The surprising finding that sector-specific models underperform due to data size should be thoroughly examined, including the methodology for comparing 'sector-agnostic' and 'sector-specific' models.

The specific examples of word ambiguity ('fire', 'beneficial') and how sector-specific models might mitigate them offer interesting linguistic insights that could be further explored for deeper understanding of the model's interpretability and limitations of general lexicons.

Key claims include the outperformance of the proposed IR term weighting, improved prediction with fusion methods, conceptual drift in 10-K reports, and the underperformance of sector-specific models due to data size, despite revealing sector-specific factors.

Assumptions include the exclusive utility of the 'Risk Factors' section, the definition of volatility, the adequacy of the finance-specific lexicon, optimality of SVR parameters, NASDAQ sector categorization, and outlier filtering methods.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents a logically coherent argument for the effectiveness of word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting, combined with market data, for predicting stock market volatility using 10-K financial disclosures. The paper systematically introduces its methodology, validates it against baselines, and then explores specific characteristics of the data (temporal drift) and model behavior (sector-specific analysis). The flow from problem identification to proposed solution, experimental validation, and nuanced analysis of findings is well-structured. The decision to focus on recent data (2012-2015) is empirically justified by the content analysis, strengthening the internal validity of subsequent experiments. While the core IR weighting scheme builds on prior work, its application and demonstrated effectiveness in this specific financial sentiment context, coupled with the detailed fusion and sectoral analyses, contribute to a robust empirical study. The paper's transparency in acknowledging limitations, such as the data size constraint for sector-specific models and slightly reduced performance in real-world prediction scenarios, enhances its credibility.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Financial volatility is a critical indicator of market instability and risk.
P2: 10-K financial disclosures contain valuable textual information for volatility prediction, specifically the 'Risk Factors' section (Assumption A1).
P3: Existing sentiment analysis methods for 10-K reports have limitations (e.g., focus on older data, less sophisticated text processing).
P4: Market data (e.g., GARCH, current volatility) are also crucial for volatility prediction.
C1: A novel word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting approach can significantly improve sentiment analysis from 10-K reports for volatility prediction (Claim C1, C6).
C2: Combining textual sentiment features with factual market data through effective fusion methods (e.g., stacking) further enhances prediction accuracy and stability (Claim C2, C7).
C3: The content of 10-K reports exhibits conceptual drifts over time, making more recent data more effective for current predictions (Claim C3).

C4: While financial sectors have distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics (Claim C9), training sector-specific models does not currently improve performance over a general model due to limited data size per sector (Claim C4).

C5: However, comparing sector-agnostic and sector-specific models reveals the existence and importance of particular risk factors in each sector, suggesting potential benefits with more data (Claim C5).
C6: Market-based features' predictive relevance decays faster over longer horizons compared to text-based features, which show more stable long-term performance (Claim C8).

Conclusion: The proposed integrated approach (word embedding-based IR + stacking fusion + recent data) offers superior and more stable volatility predictions, and insights into temporal and sectoral dynamics of financial disclosures.

The use of both r2 and MSE metrics, and clear tabular results (Table 2), provides robust evidence.

This enhances the internal validity of the experimental setup.

concerns.title: Limited Justification for Exclusive 'Risk Factors' Section Use
concerns.description: The paper assumes that only the 'Risk Factors' section (Item 1A) of 10-K reports is useful for volatility prediction, citing Dyer et al. (2016). While this is a reasonable starting point, the paper does not empirically validate this assumption for its specific task or explore whether other sections might contain complementary, non-redundant information that could further enhance prediction. This limits the scope of textual feature extraction.
evidence: "Dyer et al. (2016) ... suggest that only the risk factors topic appears to be useful and informative to investors. Their analysis motivates us to study the effectiveness of the Risk Factors section for volatility prediction."

Assumption A1: "The 'Risk Factors' section (Item 1A) of 10-K reports is the most useful and informative part for investors regarding company risk and volatility prediction, justifying its exclusive use for textual analysis."
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct an ablation study or comparative analysis to empirically evaluate the contribution of other 10-K sections (e.g., 'Management's Discussion and Analysis') to volatility prediction, or explicitly discuss the limitations of focusing solely on 'Risk Factors'.

concerns.title: Potential Loss of Information from Outlier Filtering
concerns.description: The methodology filters volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation. While intended to remove noise, this approach risks discarding genuine extreme volatility events, which are often of high interest in financial risk management. The impact of this filtering on the model's ability to predict such critical, albeit rare, events is not discussed.
evidence: "We filter the volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation of all the volatility values3."

Assumption A6: "Filtering volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation effectively removes noise/outliers without discarding meaningful extreme volatility events that could be important for risk prediction."
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a sensitivity analysis on the impact of the outlier filtering threshold or discuss the implications of this filtering on the model's performance for extreme volatility events. Consider alternative robust regression techniques less sensitive to outliers.

concerns.title: Limited Generalizability to Future Conceptual Drifts
concerns.description: The paper's strong justification for using only 2012-2015 data due to conceptual drift (Claim C3) improves internal validity for that period but raises concerns about the model's long-term generalizability. If conceptual drifts continue, a model trained on a fixed historical window might quickly become outdated. Figure 2b, showing slightly worse performance in 'real-world' prediction scenarios, hints at this challenge.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a methodology for predicting stock market volatility using sentiment from 10-K financial disclosures, enhanced by a novel word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting approach. It further investigates the benefits of fusing these textual features with traditional market data. The study rigorously analyzes temporal conceptual drifts in 10-K reports, justifying the use of more recent data, and explores the impact of sector-specific training, concluding that data scarcity limits its current utility despite evidence of distinct sector-specific risk factors. The core reasoning is that advanced textual sentiment analysis, particularly with word embedding-enhanced IR models, can capture nuanced risk signals from financial disclosures that complement and stabilize predictions derived from market data alone. The paper systematically evaluates its proposed methods against established baselines and fusion strategies, providing empirical evidence for its claims regarding improved prediction accuracy and stability over longer terms.

P8: Stacking is identified as the most effective fusion method among those tested (Claim C7, Table 1).
P9: 10-K report content exhibits conceptual drifts over time (Claim C3, Figure 1a).
P10: Using more recent data (2012-2015) for training reduces noise and improves prediction performance due to these drifts (Claim C3, Figure 1b, Assumption A7).
P11: Financial sectors have distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics (Claim C9).

concerns.description: The methodology filters out volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation. While this is a common practice to remove noise, it implicitly assumes that extreme volatility events are 'noise' rather than meaningful, albeit rare, market behaviors. If the goal is to predict all aspects of volatility, including high-impact rare events, this filtering could lead to a model that is less robust or accurate in those critical scenarios. The paper does not analyze the impact of this filtering on the model's ability to predict extreme events.
evidence: Section 5: "We filter the volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation of all the volatility values."
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the implications of outlier filtering for predicting extreme volatility events. Consider a sensitivity analysis where the filtering threshold is varied, or evaluate performance on a separate dataset of known extreme events.

While empirically justified for performance, this limits the generalizability of the findings and the trained model to earlier periods or potentially to future periods if new conceptual drifts occur. The 'real-world application' scenario partially addresses this but still relies on a growing training set from the 'most recent cluster'.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The core methodological innovation lies in the direct integration of word embeddings into IR term weighting schemes for financial sentiment analysis. specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript presents an incremental but meaningful advancement in financial volatility prediction by refining existing paradigms in sentiment analysis and feature fusion. It extends traditional Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting schemes by incorporating word embeddings, demonstrating superior performance over established baselines in extracting sentiment from 10-K reports. Furthermore, it systematically investigates and validates the effectiveness of various feature fusion methods (early, MKL, stacking) for combining textual sentiment with market data, showing that stacking yields the best results. The paper also reorganizes the understanding of financial disclosure data by empirically demonstrating conceptual drifts over time and analyzing sector-specific characteristics, providing insights into data utility and limitations of domain-specific training due to data sparsity. The contributions are primarily in the effective adaptation, integration, and empirical validation of existing techniques within the specific domain of financial volatility prediction.
logical_argument_graph: Financial volatility prediction is crucial and can benefit from sentiment analysis of textual resources like 10-K reports (Introduction).
Previous studies have used sentiment analysis on 10-K reports, often with data before 2008, and have explored lexicon expansion with word embeddings (Related Work, Introduction).
The content of 10-K reports exhibits conceptual drift over time, making older data less relevant for current prediction (C3, Figure 1a, 1b).
Therefore, using more recent and coherent data (2012-2015) is beneficial for volatility prediction (Section 6.1).
Standard IR term weighting schemes can be enhanced by extending term weights to similar words identified via word embeddings (Methodology, Section 4.1).

These extended word embedding-based IR term weighting approaches (e.g., B̂M25) significantly outperform state-of-the-art sentiment analysis methods for volatility prediction using 10-K reports (C1, C6, Table 1, Table 2).
Factual market data (e.g., GARCH, current volatility) are also valuable for volatility prediction (Section 4.2).

Combining textual sentiment features with market data through effective fusion methods (e.g., stacking) further improves prediction accuracy and stability over longer terms (C2, C7, C8, Table 1, Table 2, Figure 2a).

While financial sectors have distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics (C9), training sector-specific models does not improve performance over a general model due to limited training data size per sector (C4, Figure 3a, 3b).
However, comparing sector-agnostic and sector-specific models reveals the existence and importance of particular risk factors in each sector (C5, Figure 3a, 3b).

Overall, the proposed word embedding-based IR sentiment analysis combined with stacking fusion provides a robust and effective approach for long-term volatility forecasting using 10-K reports (Conclusion).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript introduces a novel methodology for predicting stock market volatility by enhancing sentiment analysis of 10-K financial disclosures. The central innovation lies in extending traditional Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting schemes by directly incorporating word embedding-based similarity. This approach, which weights lexicon terms by considering their similar terms within the document, is presented as a significant conceptual and empirical advancement over prior methods that primarily used word embeddings for lexicon expansion. The paper further provides a disruptive insight into the temporal dynamics of 10-K reports, demonstrating significant "conceptual drift" over time. This finding challenges the conventional wisdom of simply accumulating more data, as older, conceptually divergent reports are shown to introduce noise, leading to the strategic decision to focus on more recent data (2012-2015) for improved prediction. Additionally, the study investigates the effective fusion of these textual sentiment features with factual market data, showing that stacking methods yield superior and more stable predictions over longer horizons. An unconventional but well-supported finding is that while financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics, training sector-specific models does not outperform a general model due to data scarcity, yet the analysis still elucidates the existence and importance of these sector-specific factors.
logical_argument_graph: Financial volatility is a crucial indicator of risk, and sentiment analysis of 10-K financial reports can enhance its prediction.
Existing sentiment analysis methods for 10-K reports have limitations, particularly in how they leverage word embeddings (e.g., only for lexicon expansion).

**Proposed Innovation**: Extend IR term weighting schemes by incorporating word embedding-based similarity to weight lexicon terms based on similar terms *within the document*, aiming for more effective sentiment capture.
**Empirical Validation 1**: This extended IR term weighting approach (e.g., B̂M25) significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for volatility prediction using text-only features.
Market data (GARCH, current volatility) also predicts volatility, but its relevance decays faster over longer horizons compared to text.
**Proposed Integration**: Combine textual sentiment features with market data using various fusion methods (Early, MKL, Stacking).

**Empirical Validation 2**: Fusion methods, especially stacking, further improve prediction accuracy and stability, particularly over longer terms, demonstrating the complementary nature of text and market data.
10-K reports exhibit conceptual drift over time (e.g., 3-4 year cycles), meaning older data can introduce noise.
**Empirical Validation 3**: Using only recent, conceptually coherent data (2012-2015) improves prediction performance, supporting the conceptual drift hypothesis.
Financial sectors have distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics, suggesting potential for sector-specific models.
**Empirical Finding/Challenge**: Training sector-specific models *does not* improve performance over a general model due to insufficient data per sector.

**Insight**: However, comparison with sector-agnostic models (same data size) reveals the existence and importance of these sector-specific risk factors, indicating a future potential if more data becomes available, and showing how general models implicitly capture some of these.

**Conclusion**: The novel word embedding-based IR term weighting, combined with effective fusion, provides superior and more stable volatility predictions, and understanding the temporal and sectoral characteristics of 10-K reports is crucial.

prior_stage_inputs: The manuscript presents a logically coherent argument for the effectiveness of word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting, combined with market data, for predicting stock market volatility using 10-K financial disclosures. The flow from problem identification to proposed solution, experimental validation, and nuanced analysis of findings is well-structured. The decision to focus on recent data (2012-2015) is empirically justified by the content analysis, strengthening the internal validity of subsequent experiments. The paper presents a methodology for predicting stock market volatility using sentiment from 10-K financial disclosures, enhanced by a novel word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting approach. It further investigates the benefits of fusing these textual features with traditional market data. The study rigorously analyzes temporal conceptual drifts in 10-K reports, justifying the use of more recent data, and explores the impact of sector-specific training, concluding that data scarcity limits its current utility despite evidence of distinct sector-specific risk factors. The core reasoning is that advanced textual sentiment analysis, particularly with word embedding-enhanced IR models, can capture nuanced risk signals from financial disclosures that complement and stabilize predictions derived from market data alone. The paper systematically evaluates its proposed methods against established baselines and fusion strategies, providing empirical evidence for its claims regarding improved prediction accuracy and stability over longer terms.

The manuscript presents an incremental but meaningful advancement in financial volatility prediction by refining existing paradigms in sentiment analysis and feature fusion. It extends traditional Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting schemes by incorporating word embeddings, demonstrating superior performance over established baselines in extracting sentiment from 10-K reports. Furthermore, it systematically investigates and validates the effectiveness of various feature fusion methods (early, MKL, stacking) for combining textual sentiment with market data, showing that stacking yields the best results. The paper also reorganizes the understanding of financial disclosure data by empirically demonstrating conceptual drifts over time and analyzing sector-specific characteristics, providing insights into data utility and limitations of domain-specific training due to data sparsity. The contributions are primarily in the effective adaptation, integration, and empirical validation of existing techniques within the specific domain of financial volatility prediction.

The manuscript introduces a novel methodology for predicting stock market volatility by enhancing sentiment analysis of 10-K financial disclosures. The central innovation lies in extending traditional Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting schemes by directly incorporating word embedding-based similarity. This approach, which weights lexicon terms by considering their similar terms within the document, is presented as a significant conceptual and empirical advancement over prior methods that primarily used word embeddings for lexicon expansion. The paper further provides a disruptive insight into the temporal dynamics of 10-K reports, demonstrating significant "conceptual drift" over time. This finding challenges the conventional wisdom of simply accumulating more data, as older, conceptually divergent reports are shown to introduce noise, leading to the strategic decision to focus on more recent data (2012-2015) for improved prediction. Additionally, the study investigates the effective fusion of these textual sentiment features with factual market data, showing that stacking methods yield superior and more stable predictions over longer horizons. An unconventional but well-supported finding is that while financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics, training sector-specific models does not outperform a general model due to data scarcity, yet the analysis still elucidates the existence and importance of these sector-specific factors.
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper presents a robust empirical study on predicting stock market volatility using sentiment from 10-K financial disclosures, enhanced by a novel word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting approach. The core reasoning is that this advanced textual sentiment analysis, when effectively fused with factual market data, significantly improves prediction accuracy and stability over longer terms compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The manuscript provides strong evidence for its claims, including the outperformance of its IR term weighting scheme (C1, C6), the benefits of feature fusion (C2, C7), and the more stable predictive power of text features over market features for longer horizons (C8). Furthermore, the paper empirically demonstrates and justifies the existence of conceptual drifts in 10-K reports over time, leading to the well-supported decision to focus on more recent data for improved prediction (C3). The analysis of sector-specific characteristics is particularly insightful, showing that while distinct risk factors exist (C5, C9), training sector-specific models currently underperforms due to data scarcity (C4). The claims are generally well-supported by the presented experimental results and analyses, with minor nuances regarding the absolute generalization of performance improvements across all weighting schemes (C6) and the direct quantification of ambiguity mitigation (C9).
logical_argument_graph: Financial volatility is a key indicator of risk, and sentiment analysis of financial reports can aid its prediction (Introduction).
Previous studies on 10-K reports for volatility prediction have limitations, including focus on older data and less advanced sentiment analysis (Introduction).
The content of 10-K reports exhibits significant conceptual drifts over time, making older data less effective and introducing noise (C3, Figure 1a, 1b).
Therefore, focusing on recent, coherent data (2012-2015) is crucial for effective volatility prediction (Section 6.1).
A novel word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting approach is proposed to enhance sentiment analysis from 10-K reports (Section 4.1).

This proposed IR term weighting approach generally improves upon normal forms and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for volatility prediction using text-only features (C1, C6, Table 1, Table 2).
Factual market data (e.g., GARCH, current volatility) also provides valuable information for volatility prediction (Section 4.2).
Effective fusion methods are necessary to combine textual sentiment features with factual market data (Section 4.3).
Among tested fusion methods, stacking significantly outperforms MKL and Early Fusion, leading to further improvements in prediction accuracy and stability (C2, C7, Table 1, Table 2, Figure 2a).
Text-based features show more stable predictive relevance over longer horizons compared to market-based features, which decay faster (C8, Figure 2a).
Financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics, and sector-specific models can mitigate word ambiguity (C9, Section 6.3).
However, training sector-specific models does not improve performance over a general model due to limited training data size per sector (C4, Figures 3a, 3b, Table 3).
Comparison with sector-agnostic models confirms the existence and importance of particular risk factors in each sector, despite data limitations for specific training (C5, Figures 3a, 3b).

concerns.description: The paper exclusively uses the 'Risk Factors' section (Item 1A) of 10-K reports, citing Dyer et al. (2016) for its usefulness. However, Dyer et al. do not explicitly state that other sections lack additional, non-redundant predictive information. This assumption, while motivated, could lead to suboptimal performance if other parts of the 10-K reports contain valuable, untapped signals for volatility prediction.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct an exploratory analysis or provide a more detailed justification for the exclusive use of the 'Risk Factors' section, potentially comparing its predictive power against or in combination with other sections of the 10-K report.

concerns.description: The methodology filters volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation. While this can reduce noise, it might inadvertently remove genuine, albeit extreme, market events that are crucial for understanding and predicting high-impact volatility spikes. The impact of this filtering on the model's ability to predict such rare, significant events is not quantified.
evidence: "We filter the volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation of all the volatility values3."

Assumption A6: Filtering volatility values greater/smaller than the mean plus/minus three times the standard deviation effectively removes noise/outliers without discarding meaningful extreme volatility events that could be important for risk prediction.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a sensitivity analysis on the impact of the outlier filtering threshold. Discuss the trade-offs between noise reduction and the ability to predict extreme volatility events. Consider alternative robust methods for handling outliers or explicitly evaluate performance on extreme volatility events.

concerns.title: Limited Generalizability to Future Conceptual Drifts
concerns.description: The paper effectively identifies conceptual drifts and justifies using only 2012-2015 data for internal validity. However, this raises a concern about the generalizability of the findings to future periods, especially if new conceptual drifts occur. The 'real-world application' scenario showing slightly worse performance hints at this challenge, but a more explicit discussion on adapting to or predicting future drifts would strengthen the paper's long-term applicability.
evidence: "As shown, the most coherent and largest data consists of the subset of the reports published between 2012 to 2015. This subset is also the most recent cluster and presumably more similar to the future reports. Therefore, in the following, we only use this subset..."
Figure 2b shows 'real-world application' performance (2013, 2014, 2015) is slightly worse than cross-validation (CV).

Assumption A7: The 2012-2015 dataset, identified as the 'most coherent and largest data' and 'most recent cluster' after content analysis, is sufficiently representative for generalizing findings to future reports and market conditions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss strategies for adapting the model to future conceptual drifts, such as dynamic model retraining or incorporating drift detection mechanisms. Acknowledge the limitations of generalizing findings from a specific 3-year window to all future market conditions.

concerns.title: Lack of Detailed Hyperparameter Tuning and Sensitivity Analysis
concerns.description: The paper states that PCA dimension reduction to 400 and the choice of SVR parameters (C=1.0, ε=0.1) and RBF kernel were based on 'initial experiments' or 'previous studies'. However, detailed sensitivity analysis or a more thorough exploration of these choices is not provided. This introduces uncertainty about whether the optimal configuration was truly achieved or if different parameters could yield better or more robust results.
evidence: "Our initial experiments show 400 dimension as the optimum by trying on a range of dimensions from 50 to 1000."
"Similar to previous studies (Tsai and Wang, 2014; Kogan et al., 2009), we set C = 1.0 and = 0.1."
"Our initial experiments showed better performance of the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel in comparison to linear and cosine kernels and is therefore used in this paper."

Assumption A4: The chosen parameters for Support Vector Regression (C=1.0, ε=0.1) and the Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel are optimal or sufficiently robust for the volatility prediction task across all experiments.
Assumption A8: The use of Principle Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce feature vector dimensions to 400 is optimal and does not lead to significant loss of predictive information.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide more details on the hyperparameter tuning process (e.g., ranges explored, validation strategy). Include a sensitivity analysis for key parameters like PCA dimensions or SVR parameters to demonstrate robustness or identify potential for further optimization.

concerns.title: Unquantified Impact of Stemming Choices
concerns.description: The paper uses the Porter stemmer for text preprocessing. While a common choice, stemming can sometimes lead to over-stemming or loss of nuanced semantic distinctions, which might be particularly relevant in the context of financial sentiment where subtle word differences can carry significant meaning. The impact of this stemming choice on sentiment feature quality and prediction accuracy is not evaluated.
evidence: "...stemmed using the Porter stemmer."
"Finally, the texts are stemmed using the Porter stemmer."

Assumption A9: The Porter stemmer is appropriate for financial text, and its stemming rules do not introduce significant semantic loss or ambiguity for sentiment analysis, particularly for risk-sensitive terms.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Briefly discuss the potential implications of stemming choices in financial text. Consider a small-scale comparison with alternative preprocessing (e.g., lemmatization or no stemming) or a qualitative analysis of how stemming affects key risk-sensitive terms.

uncertainty_flags: The paper acknowledges that sector-specific models underperform due to limited data size, suggesting that this finding might change with more extensive sector-specific data, introducing uncertainty about the ultimate utility of sector-specific models.

The 'real-world application' scenario (predicting future years based on past data) shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation, indicating potential challenges in out-of-sample prediction and generalizability to truly unseen future data.

The implementation details for the GARCH model are moved to supplementary materials, which introduces a slight uncertainty regarding its exact setup and potential impact on baseline comparisons without full access to those details.

The choice of a fixed cosine similarity threshold (0.70) for word embedding-based term weighting is cited from prior work but not empirically validated for this specific task, introducing uncertainty about its optimality.

The impact of filtering extreme volatility values (mean +/- 3 std dev) on the model's ability to predict genuine, high-impact rare events is not quantified, leading to uncertainty about its robustness in such scenarios.

The optimality of SVR parameters (C=1.0, ε=0.1) and the RBF kernel is stated based on 'initial experiments' without detailed sensitivity analysis, introducing some uncertainty about whether peak performance was achieved.
alternative_interpretations: The observed 'conceptual drifts' in 10-K reports (C3) could be partially attributed to evolving regulatory requirements or changes in corporate reporting standards, rather than solely intrinsic shifts in company risk factors or communication styles. While the paper attributes it to 'noise', a deeper analysis of the drivers of these drifts could offer alternative interpretations.

The underperformance of sector-specific models (C4) might not be *solely* due to data size. It's possible that the NASDAQ categorization of sectors (Assumption A5) is too broad, or that the 'general model' implicitly captures broader economic factors that are more predictive than highly granular sector-specific nuances, even with sufficient data.

While sector-specific models are shown to mitigate ambiguity (C9) qualitatively, the lack of quantitative improvement in overall sector-specific prediction (C4) suggests that the impact of ambiguity mitigation on overall predictive performance might be minor compared to the benefits of a larger, more diverse training set from a general model.
transparency_notes: The paper is transparent about its dataset sources (SEC, Yahoo Finance) and the specific section of 10-K reports used ('Risk Factors').
The authors explicitly state the parameters used for SVR (C=1.0, ε=0.1) and BM25 (k=1.2, b=0.65), and the choice of RBF kernel, citing previous studies or initial experiments.
The decision to use only 2012-2015 data is clearly justified by the content analysis and empirical results regarding conceptual drift.
The paper acknowledges the limitation of data size for sector-specific models and provides a comparative analysis with sector-agnostic models to support this finding.
The distinction between cross-validation and 'real-world application' performance is presented, offering a more realistic view of model generalizability.

consensus_findings: The proposed word embedding-based Information Retrieval (IR) term weighting approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods for volatility prediction using financial disclosure sentiments (Claim C1, C6).

Effective fusion methods, particularly stacking, combining textual sentiment features from 10-K reports with factual market data, further improve volatility prediction accuracy and stability over longer terms (Claim C2, C7).
The content of 10-K reports exhibits significant conceptual drifts over time, making more recent data (e.g., 2012-2015) more effective for current volatility prediction by reducing noise (Claim C3).

While financial sectors exhibit distinct risk-sensitive term characteristics and sector-specific models can mitigate word ambiguity, training sector-specific models does not improve performance over a general model due to limited training data size per sector (Claim C4, C5, C9).
Market-based features decrease in predictive relevance faster over longer prediction horizons compared to text-based features, which show more stable performance (Claim C8).
disagreements: There is a controlled disagreement among reviewers regarding the *degree* of novelty of the word embedding-based IR term weighting approach. Some reviewers perceive it as a 'conceptual innovation' or 'disruptive insight' (Reviewer 4), highlighting its distinctness from mere lexicon expansion. Others view it as an 'incremental but meaningful advancement' or 'effective refinement' (Reviewer 3), acknowledging its strong empirical performance but situating it within existing paradigms of word embedding integration and IR models.
uncertainty_hotspots: The generalizability of findings to future conceptual drifts is uncertain, as the model relies on a fixed 'most recent cluster' (2012-2015) and 'real-world application' shows slightly worse performance than cross-validation.

The reproducibility of the word embedding model (Word2Vec) and specific preprocessing steps (e.g., term matching heuristics for 'Risk Factors' section, Porter stemmer version) is limited due to missing details.

The optimality and robustness of key hyperparameters (SVR parameters, PCA dimensions, cosine similarity threshold for word embeddings) are uncertain, as their selection is based on 'initial experiments' or 'previous studies' without detailed tuning or sensitivity analysis.

Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: Q: Can I use generative AI?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, policy_screen
Content: cs committee is currently developing a full process for investigating and taking action on scientific malpractice, similar to the process for investigating professional misconduct. There is already a policy on review incentives and sanctions, including temporary bans on (re-)submission or commitment to ACL venues. To add to the above points, the reviews that look like they were written by ChatGPT overall decrease the faith in the peer review process. According to this study, there is more generated text in ‘reviews which report lower confidence, were submitted close to the deadline, and from reviewers who are less likely to respond to author rebuttals’. All these factors generally correspond to the type of unmotivated reviewer that, as authors, we would prefer to avoid. The increased ratio of such reviews also attunes the community to reviews that sound like they were generated. Generally, reviews are valued for their content rather than language, so your thoughts are more likely to be appreciated if they come in your voice (even if with linguistic imperfections). Finally: some authors actually count on you to use generative AI, and include hidden prompt injections intended to manipulate your assistant into giving a positive review! If you notice anything like that, please raise it with the chairs, such submissions should be desk rejected. What about the authors, can they use generative AI? The ACL policy on publication ethics discusses various cases with different degrees of acceptability.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.
